# Using the rural observatory data to assess the protected areas impacts on household living conditions.

This document presents the first steps of an evaluation of the socio-economic impacts of protected areas in Madagascar, based on the Rural Observatory Surveys (ROS) conducted between 1995 and 2015. These longitudinal household surveys offer a rare opportunity to study rural livelihoods over two decades. By linking the ROS to official administrative boundaries and protected area limits, we want to analyze how conservation policies intersect with local livelihoods. 

This work combines several methodoligcal approaches to identify impacts of protected areas. The aim is to produce a transparent and reproducible workflow, where each chapter builds the foundations for robust causal analysis, from data cleaning to impact estimation. The provisional results are exploratory, but they already provide insights into the complex and often non-linear relationships between conservation policies and household living conditions.

The document is composed by the following sections:

- [ROS historical data georeferencing](01_Georeference_observatories.qmd). The available ROS surveys (1995–2015) were not precisely georeferenced and contained variations in place names. We applied a cleaning process and fuzzy matching based on the Common Operational Datasets (CODs) to link each observation to the official communes and fokontany.
- [Overlaps between ROS data and PAs](02_Overlaps_PAs_observatories.qmd). Here we analyze the overlap between ROS sites (1995–2015) and the protected areas of the SAPM. Some PAs existed before the surveys, two were created during the survey period, and several after the monitoring ended. This analysis led us to prioritize the Marovoay/Ankarafantsika and Alaotra/Alaotra-CAZ observatory/protected area pairs.
- [Variable computation](03_Variable computation.qmd) calculates and compounds household-level variables from the ROS surveys (1995–2015), covering georeferencing, demographics, education, food security, activities, and income. We systematically address inconsistencies across years—such as changing identifiers, missing modules, and shifts in questionnaire design—while reconstructing comparable indicators at the household level. The result is a consolidated dataset, including partial income measures, that provides a consistent basis for analyzing the impact of protected areas on rural livelihoods over time.
- [Marovoay-Ankarafantsika](04_Marovoay-Ankarafantsika.qmd) section assesses the socio-economic impacts of the 2002 expansion of Ankarafantsika into a national park, combining historical context, spatial mapping of survey sites, and reconstruction of household panels. Treated and control groups were defined across the Betsiboka river and extended to other observatories, and synthetic control methods were applied to income and welfare indicators. At this very preliminary stage, results show no robust positive effects, with agricultural revenues slightly negatively affected and no consistent changes in diversification, food self-sufficiency, or schooling.
